completion_data.completion_summary: Fixed Stage 8 postflight's truncating .return-meta.json write (both clean-exit and partial-exit paths) with a jq recursive-merge read-modify-write, added modified_count accounting plus the canonical fail-safe warning at CHECKPOINT 3 in orchestrate.md, documented the multiple-sequential-writers invariant in return-metadata-file.md with a cross-reference from git-staging-scope.md, and proved the fix end-to-end with a 19-assertion executable harness that produces real git commits asserted via git show --name-only, plus the zero-modified_files negative case.

memory_candidates.content: Shared per-task state files written by more than one process in a single orchestration run (e.g. .return-meta.json, written first by an implementation agent and again by the orchestrator skill's own postflight) must use read-modify-write merges, not truncating `jq -n ... > file` redirects. jq's recursive-merge operator `. * {...}` piped through mktemp+mv gives field preservation (including nested sub-object fields like metadata.agent_type) for free, and is strictly better than a two-line `.status = ... | .metadata.x = ...` assignment chain, which still discards untouched sub-object fields. Defect signature to watch for: a later writer's snippet uses `jq -n` (null input) plus a `>` redirect onto a path an earlier writer already populated.

When a bash test harness registers scratch directories for cleanup via `trap ... EXIT`, the registration function MUST NOT be invoked via command substitution (`x=$(register_and_build_scratch)`) if it appends to an in-memory array for the trap to consume later -- command substitution runs in a subshell, so an array append inside it is invisible to the parent shell's trap. Register scratch paths via a manifest FILE (appended with `>>`) instead, since file writes survive the subshell boundary. This silently leaked dozens of /tmp directories across repeated harness runs before being caught by an explicit post-run 'is /tmp clean' check.

A stderr redirect placed after the closing `)` of a `$(...)` command substitution used in a variable assignment (`out=$(cmd) 2>file`) does NOT capture the substitution's own stderr -- command substitution is expanded during word-expansion, before the assignment statement's own redirections are set up, so the subshell's fd 2 is still the parent's terminal/fd. To capture both stdout (via the assignment) and stderr (to a file) from the same subshell, wrap the body in an explicit compound command and attach the redirect there: `out=$({ cmd; } 2>file)`.
